title: Sum of two integers
statement:
You are given two integers a and b. Print their sum.

Input
The only line contains two integers `a` and `b` (`-10^9 â‰¤ a, b â‰¤ 10^9`).

Output
Print one integer: `a + b`.

Note
The sum can reach `2Â·10^9` in absolute value, which does not fit in a signed 32-bit integer. Use a 64-bit type in C, C++, Java and Go.
editorial: Read both values and print their sum. The only trap is overflow: `10^9 + 10^9` is outside the 32-bit range, so accumulate in `long long`, `long` or `int64`.
reference:
import sys
a,b=map(int,sys.stdin.read().split())
print(a+b)
wrong:
import sys
a,b=map(int,sys.stdin.read().split())
print(a-b)

title: Larger of two
statement:
You are given two integers a and b. Print the larger of them. If they are equal, print that common value.

Input
The only line contains two integers `a` and `b` (`-10^9 â‰¤ a, b â‰¤ 10^9`).

Output
Print `max(a, b)`.
editorial: One comparison is enough. Equal values need no special case, because printing either one is correct.
reference:
import sys
a,b=map(int,sys.stdin.read().split())
print(a if a>=b else b)
wrong:
import sys
a,b=map(int,sys.stdin.read().split())
print(a if a<=b else b)

title: Even or odd
statement:
Determine whether the integer n is even or odd.

Input
The only line contains an integer `n` (`-10^9 â‰¤ n â‰¤ 10^9`).

Output
Print `even` if n is divisible by 2, and `odd` otherwise.

Note
Zero is even. In C, C++, Java and Go the remainder of a negative odd number divided by 2 is `-1`, not `1`, so compare the remainder with zero.
editorial: Check `n mod 2 = 0`. Testing `n mod 2 = 1` instead fails for negative odd numbers in languages whose remainder takes the sign of the dividend.
reference:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
print("even" if n%2==0 else "odd")
wrong:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
print("even")

title: Sum of a list
statement:
You are given an array of n integers. Print the sum of its elements.

Input
The first line contains an integer `n` (`1 â‰¤ n â‰¤ 2Â·10^5`), the length of the array.
The second line contains n integers `a_1, a_2, â€¦, a_n` (`-10^9 â‰¤ a_i â‰¤ 10^9`).

Output
Print one integer: `a_1 + a_2 + â€¦ + a_n`.

Note
The sum can reach `2Â·10^14` in absolute value. Use a 64-bit accumulator.
editorial: Read n, then add the next n values. The length itself is not part of the sum. A 32-bit accumulator overflows on large tests.
reference:
import sys
data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
print(sum(data[1:1+data[0]]))
wrong:
import sys
data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
print(sum(data))

title: Reverse the word
statement:
You are given a word s consisting of lowercase Latin letters. Print s written backwards.

Input
The only line contains the string `s` (`1 â‰¤ |s| â‰¤ 5Â·10^4`).

Output
Print the characters of s in reverse order.
editorial: Walk the string from the last character to the first, or use the languageâ€™s reverse routine. A one-letter word and a palindrome are unchanged.
reference:
import sys
print(sys.stdin.read().strip()[::-1])
wrong:
import sys
print(sys.stdin.read().strip())

title: Count the vowels
statement:
You are given a word s of Latin letters in upper or lower case. Count its vowels. The vowels are `a`, `e`, `i`, `o` and `u` in either case; `y` is not a vowel.

Input
The only line contains the string `s` (`1 â‰¤ |s| â‰¤ 10^5`), consisting of uppercase and lowercase Latin letters.

Output
Print one integer: the number of vowels in s.
editorial: Lower-case each character and test membership in `aeiou`. Forgetting the upper-case vowels is the usual mistake.
reference:
import sys
s=sys.stdin.read().strip().lower()
print(sum(ch in "aeiou" for ch in s))
wrong:
import sys
s=sys.stdin.read().strip()
print(sum(ch in "aeiou" for ch in s))

title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
statement:
Convert a temperature from degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit using integer arithmetic.

Input
The only line contains an integer `C` (`-273 â‰¤ C â‰¤ 10^4`).

Output
Print `âŒŠ9Â·C / 5âŒ‹ + 32`, where `âŒŠxâŒ‹` is the largest integer not greater than x.

Note
The division rounds down, toward negative infinity: for `C = -1` the answer is `âŒŠ-9/5âŒ‹ + 32 = -2 + 32 = 30`. In C, C++, Java and Go integer division rounds toward zero, so negative temperatures need care.
editorial: Compute `9Â·C` and divide by 5, rounding down. Pythonâ€™s `//` already floors. Elsewhere, subtract one from the truncated quotient when `9Â·C` is negative and not a multiple of 5.
reference:
import sys
c=int(sys.stdin.read())
print(c*9//5+32)
wrong:
import sys
c=int(sys.stdin.read())
print(int(c*9/5)+32)

title: One number of FizzBuzz
statement:
For a positive integer n, print `FizzBuzz` if n is divisible by both 3 and 5, `Fizz` if it is divisible by 3 only, `Buzz` if it is divisible by 5 only, and the number n itself otherwise.

Input
The only line contains an integer `n` (`1 â‰¤ n â‰¤ 10^9`).

Output
Print the word described above, or the number n.
editorial: Test divisibility by 15 first. Checking 3 before 15 reports every multiple of 15 as `Fizz`.
reference:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
print("FizzBuzz" if n%15==0 else "Fizz" if n%3==0 else "Buzz" if n%5==0 else n)
wrong:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
print("Fizz" if n%3==0 else "Buzz" if n%5==0 else "FizzBuzz" if n%15==0 else n)

title: Digit sum
statement:
Print the sum of the decimal digits of a non-negative integer n.

Input
The only line contains an integer `n` (`0 ≤ n ≤ 10^18`).

Output
Print one integer: the sum of the digits of n.

Note
n can exceed the 32-bit range. Read it as a 64-bit integer or as a string.
editorial: Take the last digit with `n mod 10` and drop it with integer division by 10 until n is zero, or sum the characters of the string. Zero has digit sum zero.
reference:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
print(sum(int(ch) for ch in str(n)))
wrong:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
print(n%9)

title: Absolute difference
statement:
You are given two integers a and b. Print the distance between them on the number line, `|a − b|`.

Input
The only line contains two integers `a` and `b` (`-10^9 ≤ a, b ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print one integer: `|a − b|`.

Note
The answer can reach `2·10^9`, which does not fit in a signed 32-bit integer.
editorial: Subtract and drop the sign. Equal numbers give zero. Compute in 64 bits, because `10^9 − (−10^9)` overflows a 32-bit integer.
reference:
import sys
a,b=map(int,sys.stdin.read().split())
print(abs(a-b))
wrong:
import sys
a,b=map(int,sys.stdin.read().split())
print(a-b)

title: Palindrome word
statement:
A palindrome reads the same from left to right and from right to left. Determine whether the word s is a palindrome.

Input
The only line contains the string `s` (`1 ≤ |s| ≤ 10^5`) of lowercase Latin letters.

Output
Print `yes` if s is a palindrome, and `no` otherwise.
editorial: Compare `s[i]` with `s[|s| − 1 − i]` for every i in the first half, or compare the string with its reverse. Checking only the end characters is not enough.
reference:
import sys
s=sys.stdin.read().strip()
print("yes" if s==s[::-1] else "no")
wrong:
import sys
s=sys.stdin.read().strip()
print("yes" if s[0]==s[-1] else "no")

title: Minimum of a list
statement:
You are given an array of n integers. Print its smallest element.

Input
The first line contains an integer `n` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10^5`).
The second line contains n integers `a_1, a_2, …, a_n` (`-10^9 ≤ a_i ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print `min(a_1, …, a_n)`.
editorial: Keep the smallest value seen while scanning. Start from the first element, not from zero or from n, which is not part of the array.
reference:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
print(min(d[1:1+d[0]]))
wrong:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
print(min(d))

title: Greatest common divisor
statement:
Find the greatest common divisor of two positive integers a and b: the largest integer that divides both of them.

Input
The only line contains two integers `a` and `b` (`1 ≤ a, b ≤ 10^18`).

Output
Print `gcd(a, b)`.
editorial: Euclid’s algorithm: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)` and `gcd(a, 0) = a`. It needs `O(log min(a, b))` steps, so 64-bit inputs are no problem. Trying every divisor is far too slow at `10^18`.
reference:
import sys
import math
a,b=map(int,sys.stdin.read().split())
print(math.gcd(a,b))
wrong:
import sys
a,b=map(int,sys.stdin.read().split())
print(min(a,b))

title: Prime check
statement:
Determine whether the integer n is prime. A prime has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself.

Input
The only line contains an integer `n` (`2 ≤ n ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print `yes` if n is prime, and `no` otherwise.
editorial: A composite n has a divisor d with `2 ≤ d ≤ √n`, so trial division up to `⌊√n⌋` (inclusive) decides it in about 31623 steps. Stopping one short misses perfect squares of primes such as 9.
reference:
import sys
import math
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
ok=all(n%d for d in range(2,math.isqrt(n)+1))
print("yes" if ok else "no")
wrong:
import sys
import math
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
ok=all(n%d for d in range(2,math.isqrt(n)))
print("yes" if ok else "no")

title: Fibonacci number
statement:
The Fibonacci numbers are defined by `F(0) = 0`, `F(1) = 1` and `F(k) = F(k − 1) + F(k − 2)` for `k ≥ 2`. Given n, print `F(n)`.

Input
The only line contains an integer `n` (`0 ≤ n ≤ 90`).

Output
Print `F(n)`.

Note
`F(90) = 2880067194370816120`, which fits in a signed 64-bit integer.
editorial: Keep the last two values and step forward n times. Plain recursion takes exponential time, and the values need 64 bits.
reference:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
a,b=0,1
for _ in range(n):
 a,b=b,a+b
print(a)
wrong:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
a,b=1,1
for _ in range(n):
 a,b=b,a+b
print(a)

title: Count distinct
statement:
You are given an array of n integers. Print how many different values it contains.

Input
The first line contains an integer `n` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10^5`).
The second line contains n integers `a_1, a_2, …, a_n` (`-10^9 ≤ a_i ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print the number of distinct values among `a_1, …, a_n`.
editorial: Insert every value into a hash set and print its size, or sort and count the positions where the value changes. Counting changes without sorting is wrong when equal values are not adjacent.
reference:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
print(len(set(d[1:1+d[0]])))
wrong:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
a=d[1:1+d[0]]
print(1+sum(a[i]!=a[i-1] for i in range(1,len(a))))

title: Longest run
statement:
A run is a maximal block of equal consecutive characters. Given a string s of lowercase Latin letters, print the length of its longest run.

Input
The only line contains the string `s` (`1 ≤ |s| ≤ 2·10^5`).

Output
Print one integer: the length of the longest run in s.
editorial: Scan once, extending the current run while the character repeats and resetting it to 1 otherwise; remember the maximum. The most frequent character is not the answer, because its occurrences need not be consecutive.
reference:
import sys
s=sys.stdin.read().strip()
best=run=1
for i in range(1,len(s)):
 run=run+1 if s[i]==s[i-1] else 1
 best=max(best,run)
print(best)
wrong:
import sys
s=sys.stdin.read().strip()
print(max(s.count(c) for c in set(s)))

title: Balanced brackets
statement:
A bracket sequence is balanced if its brackets can be paired so that every `(` is matched with a later `)` and the pairs are properly nested. For example, `(())()` is balanced, while `)(` and `(()` are not. Decide whether the sequence s is balanced.

Input
The only line contains the string `s` (`1 ≤ |s| ≤ 10^5`), consisting of the characters `(` and `)`.

Output
Print `yes` if s is balanced, and `no` otherwise.
editorial: Keep a depth counter: add one for `(` and subtract one for `)`. The sequence is balanced exactly when the depth never drops below zero and ends at zero. Equal counts alone are not enough, as `)(` shows.
reference:
import sys
s=sys.stdin.read().strip()
d=0
ok=True
for ch in s:
 d+=1 if ch=="(" else -1
 if d<0: ok=False
print("yes" if ok and d==0 else "no")
wrong:
import sys
s=sys.stdin.read().strip()
print("yes" if s.count("(")==s.count(")") else "no")

title: Pair with a given sum
statement:
You are given an array of n integers and an integer t. Determine whether there are two different positions `i ≠ j` such that `a_i + a_j = t`.

Input
The first line contains two integers `n` and `t` (`2 ≤ n ≤ 2·10^5`, `-2·10^9 ≤ t ≤ 2·10^9`).
The second line contains n integers `a_1, a_2, …, a_n` (`-10^9 ≤ a_i ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print `yes` if such a pair exists, and `no` otherwise.

Note
The positions must differ, but the values may be equal: for `a = [3, 3]` and `t = 6` the answer is `yes`, while for `a = [3, 5]` and `t = 6` it is `no`.
editorial: Scan once with a hash set of the values seen so far. Before inserting `a_i`, check whether `t − a_i` is already in the set; checking after inserting would pair an element with itself. Sorting and two pointers also works in `O(n log n)`.
reference:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
n,t=d[0],d[1]
seen=set()
ok=False
for x in d[2:2+n]:
 if t-x in seen:
  ok=True
  break
 seen.add(x)
print("yes" if ok else "no")
wrong:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
n,t=d[0],d[1]
s=set(d[2:2+n])
print("yes" if any(t-x in s for x in s) else "no")

title: Range sum
statement:
You are given an array of n integers and q queries. Each query gives two indices l and r; answer it with the sum `a_l + a_{l+1} + … + a_r`.

Input
The first line contains two integers `n` and `q` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10^5`, `1 ≤ q ≤ 3000`).
The second line contains n integers `a_1, a_2, …, a_n` (`-10^9 ≤ a_i ≤ 10^9`).
Each of the next q lines contains two integers `l` and `r` (`1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n`).

Output
For each query, print the sum on its own line.
editorial: Build prefix sums `p_0 = 0`, `p_i = p_{i−1} + a_i` once. A query is then `p_r − p_{l−1}` in constant time. Summing each range directly costs up to `n·q = 6·10^8` operations. Sums reach `2·10^14`, so use 64-bit integers.
reference:
import sys
d=sys.stdin.read().split()
it=iter(d)
n,q=int(next(it)),int(next(it))
a=[int(next(it)) for _ in range(n)]
p=[0]
for x in a: p.append(p[-1]+x)
out=[]
for _ in range(q):
 l,r=int(next(it)),int(next(it))
 out.append(str(p[r]-p[l-1]))
print("\n".join(out))
wrong:
import sys
d=sys.stdin.read().split()
it=iter(d)
n,q=int(next(it)),int(next(it))
a=[int(next(it)) for _ in range(n)]
p=[0]
for x in a: p.append(p[-1]+x)
out=[]
for _ in range(q):
 l,r=int(next(it)),int(next(it))
 out.append(str(p[r]-p[l]))
print("\n".join(out))

title: Climbing stairs
statement:
A staircase has n steps. With each move you climb either one step or two. Count the different sequences of moves that take you from the bottom exactly to the top.

Input
The only line contains an integer `n` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 90`).

Output
Print the number of ways. It fits in a signed 64-bit integer.
editorial: The last move is one step or two, so `ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2)` with `ways(0) = ways(1) = 1`. That is the Fibonacci sequence shifted by one: `ways(n) = F(n + 1)`.
reference:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
a,b=1,1
for _ in range(n):
 a,b=b,a+b
print(a)
wrong:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
a,b=0,1
for _ in range(n):
 a,b=b,a+b
print(a)

title: Rotate left
statement:
You are given an array of n integers and an integer k. Rotate the array left by k positions, that is, move the first element to the end k times, and print the result.

Input
The first line contains two integers `n` and `k` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 5000`, `0 ≤ k ≤ 10^9`).
The second line contains n integers `a_1, a_2, …, a_n` (`-10^9 ≤ a_i ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print the n elements of the rotated array, separated by spaces.

Note
k may be much larger than n. Rotating by a multiple of n leaves the array unchanged.
editorial: Only `k mod n` matters. Print `a_{s+1}, …, a_n` followed by `a_1, …, a_s` with `s = k mod n`. Simulating k single moves is far too slow at `k = 10^9`.
reference:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
n,k=d[0],d[1]%d[0]
a=d[2:2+n]
a=a[k:]+a[:k]
print(*a)
wrong:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
n,k=d[0],d[1]
a=d[2:2+n]
a=a[k:]+a[:k]
print(*a)

title: Maximum subarray
statement:
You are given an array of n integers. Find the largest possible sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray `a_l, a_{l+1}, …, a_r`.

Input
The first line contains an integer `n` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10^5`).
The second line contains n integers `a_1, a_2, …, a_n` (`-10^9 ≤ a_i ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print the maximum subarray sum.

Note
The subarray must contain at least one element, so when every number is negative the answer is the largest of them.
editorial: Kadane’s algorithm: the best sum ending at position i is either `a_i` alone or `a_i` plus the best sum ending at `i − 1`. Track the maximum over all i. Initialising the answer to 0 is wrong when every element is negative.
reference:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
a=d[1:1+d[0]]
best=cur=a[0]
for x in a[1:]:
 cur=max(x,cur+x)
 best=max(best,cur)
print(best)
wrong:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
a=d[1:1+d[0]]
best=cur=0
for x in a:
 cur=max(0,cur+x)
 best=max(best,cur)
print(best)

title: Bounded knapsack
statement:
There are n items. Item i has weight `w_i` and value `v_i`. Choose a set of items, each taken at most once, whose total weight does not exceed W and whose total value is as large as possible.

Input
The first line contains two integers `n` and `W` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 100`, `1 ≤ W ≤ 10^4`).
Each of the next n lines contains two integers `w_i` and `v_i` (`1 ≤ w_i ≤ 10^4`, `1 ≤ v_i ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print the largest total value of a set of items with total weight at most W.
editorial: Let `best[c]` be the largest value with weight at most c. Process items one by one and update c from W down to `w_i`: `best[c] = max(best[c], best[c − w_i] + v_i)`. Going downwards uses each item at most once. This is `O(n·W)`. Taking items greedily by value per unit weight is not optimal.
reference:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
n,W=d[0],d[1]
best=[0]*(W+1)
for i in range(n):
 w,v=d[2+2*i],d[3+2*i]
 if w<=W:
  best=best[:w]+[max(x,y+v) for x,y in zip(best[w:],best)]
print(best[W])
wrong:
import sys
d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.read().split()))
n,W=d[0],d[1]
items=sorted(((d[2+2*i],d[3+2*i]) for i in range(n)),key=lambda p:-p[1]/p[0])
total=used=0
for w,v in items:
 if used+w<=W:
  used+=w
  total+=v
print(total)

title: Shortest path in a line
statement:
You are given an undirected graph with n vertices numbered from 1 to n and m edges. Find the minimum number of edges on a path from vertex 1 to vertex n.

Input
The first line contains two integers `n` and `m` (`2 ≤ n ≤ 10^5`, `0 ≤ m ≤ 2·10^5`).
Each of the next m lines contains two integers `u` and `v` (`1 ≤ u, v ≤ n`), an edge between u and v. The graph may contain loops and multiple edges.

Output
Print the length of the shortest path, or `-1` if vertex n cannot be reached from vertex 1.
editorial: Breadth-first search from vertex 1 visits vertices in order of distance, so the first time it reaches n the distance is minimal. Store each edge in both directions; treating the graph as directed fails when an edge is listed as `v u`. The search is `O(n + m)`.
reference:
import sys
from collections import deque
d=sys.stdin.read().split()
it=iter(d)
n,m=int(next(it)),int(next(it))
g=[[] for _ in range(n+1)]
for _ in range(m):
 u,v=int(next(it)),int(next(it))
 g[u].append(v)
 g[v].append(u)
dist=[-1]*(n+1)
dist[1]=0
q=deque([1])
while q:
 u=q.popleft()
 for v in g[u]:
  if dist[v]<0:
   dist[v]=dist[u]+1
   q.append(v)
print(dist[n])
wrong:
import sys
from collections import deque
d=sys.stdin.read().split()
it=iter(d)
n,m=int(next(it)),int(next(it))
g=[[] for _ in range(n+1)]
for _ in range(m):
 u,v=int(next(it)),int(next(it))
 g[u].append(v)
dist=[-1]*(n+1)
dist[1]=0
q=deque([1])
while q:
 u=q.popleft()
 for v in g[u]:
  if dist[v]<0:
   dist[v]=dist[u]+1
   q.append(v)
print(dist[n])

title: Partial double
statement:
Print twice the given integer n.

Input
The only line contains an integer `n` (`-10^9 ≤ n ≤ 10^9`).

Output
Print `2·n`.

Scoring
The tests form two groups. Group `sample` (30 points) contains only non-negative n. Group `full` (70 points) contains any n. Each group is scored on its own, so a solution that handles only non-negative n still earns 30 points.
editorial: Multiply by two in 64-bit arithmetic: `2·10^9` does not fit in a signed 32-bit integer. A solution that mishandles negative input passes the `sample` group only.
reference:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
print(n*2)
wrong:
import sys
n=int(sys.stdin.read())
print(n*2 if n>=0 else n)
